analysis.one_liner: Restores the legal wall separating commercial banking from securities underwriting and trading.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee from July 2011 until Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have re-imposed core parts of the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act: it would have barred banks that take insured deposits from being affiliated with companies whose main business is underwriting, selling, or distributing stocks and bonds, and barred the same person from serving as an officer of both a bank and such a securities firm. Banks would have had one year to break those ties, though the Federal Reserve could grant limited exceptions. The stated aim is to keep depositors' insured money and public bailout backing away from securities-market risk.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary bank depositors and taxpayers, who would no longer have federally insured deposits and implicit government backing standing behind securities underwriting and trading arms; smaller community banks, which would compete against conglomerates without those ties.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits member banks from being affiliated with any company engaged principally in issuing, underwriting, publicly selling, or distributing stocks, bonds, or other securities, effective one year after enactment [S2][S3].
Bars any individual from simultaneously serving as an officer, director, or employee of a securities underwriting firm and of a member bank, subject to limited Federal Reserve exceptions [S2][S3].
Allows formal liquidation: an affiliated securities organization placed in formal liquidation and doing no other business is exempt from the affiliation ban [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large universal banks and their shareholders, which would have had one year to divest or spin off securities underwriting and distribution businesses; combined bank-securities firms would lose the cost advantages and scale of operating insured deposits and securities businesses under one roof.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large universal banks and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: Banks would have only one year to unwind existing bank-securities affiliations, a deadline that could force rushed divestitures or restructurings of major financial firms [S3].

A widely voiced objection from the banking industry and some economists was that reinstating the separation would not have prevented the 2008 crisis, whose largest failures involved firms and activities the Glass-Steagall wall never covered; defenders respond that the wall limited contagion and taxpayer exposure rather than preventing all failures.

Breaking up universal banks could raise some costs for large corporate clients that rely on a single institution for both lending and securities issuance; retail depositors would see little direct change in their banking services.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but one-sided: the cost falls on a small number of very large financial firms and their shareholders, while the benefit — reducing the chance that insured deposits and government backstops absorb securities-market losses — accrues broadly to depositors and taxpayers. The one-year divestiture timeline was aggressive and could have caused disruption, but the Federal Reserve's limited-exception authority gave regulators a release valve. On balance, a straightforward consumer-and-taxpayer protection measure with concentrated costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on July 7, 2011, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Conyers, Inslee, DeFazio, Woolsey, and Capuano [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services, and no further action of any kind appears in the record [S5].
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without a subcommittee or full committee vote, a floor debate, or a roll call [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest universal banks kept combining insured deposits with securities underwriting and trading, preserving the structure the bill would have dismantled; depositors and taxpayers continue to bear the underlying risk the bill sought to remove.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large universal banks kept the status quo

for.name: Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Glass-Steagall Restoration Act of 2011 in the House.

for.name: John Conyers, Peter DeFazio, Jay Inslee, Lynn Woolsey, and Michael Capuano
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it six total House supporters and no other endorsements.

against.name: Spencer Bachus
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to, which held no hearing, mark-up, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — six House Democrats and no Republican sponsors or cosponsors — and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Universal banks and bank holding companies combining insured deposits with securities businesses
industries.note: The bill would have forced them, within one year, to divest or spin off securities underwriting and distribution operations and barred shared officers. Their business model profits from running deposit-taking and securities operations under one roof, which is exactly the structure the bill targets, so their interest runs against the depositor protection the bill offers.

industries.industry: Securities underwriting and distribution firms affiliated with banks
industries.note: Firms principally engaged in issuing, underwriting, and selling securities would lose bank affiliations, and their personnel could no longer sit as officers or employees of member banks. Bank-affiliated underwriters would need to operate separately or be liquidated.

industries.industry: Community and regional banks without securities affiliates
industries.note: These banks already operate without bank-securities affiliations, so they would face little compliance burden while their largest conglomerate competitors shed scale advantages. Their interest in the bill runs alongside depositors'.
